latin.408: Reliqua quae addit hoc loco vir doctus egere non videntur refutatione, praesertim si memineris, candide lector, eorum quae dicta sunt a nobis supra pag. 163. Cum assertionem, voluntatem Adami fuisse voluntatem omnium, oppugnavi, non putabam illius hunc esse sensum, volitionem, quam Adamus circa arborem vetitam exercuit, omnibus imputari. Sequentia Thomae verba quae tu adscripsisti etsi verum continent praetermittenda non sunt. Et sicut peccatum actuale, quod est peccatum personae, trahitur ad singula membra per aliquem actum personalem, ita peccatum originale trahitur ad singulos homines per actum naturae qui est generatio. Rursus peccatum actuale distinguit ab originali, & utrumque vult in Adamo fuisse: illud personae, hoc naturae. Necesse est igitur ut per originale corruptionem intelligat ex peccato actuali ortam. Quare non voluit peccatum actuale, quod personae est, nobis imputari: immo nec vitium naturae quatenus in Adamo haesit, ut mox videbimus: alioqui imputanda etiam nobis esset generatio, qua secundum nostrum parentem Sethum Adamus genuit, quandoquidem illa teste Thoma actus fuit naturae. Subjicit, Et ita sicut per generationem humana natura trahitur, ita etiam per generationem traducitur defectus humanae naturae qui est consecutus ex peccato primi parentis. Nihil verius. Mea haec est sententia. Unde concludo, quemadmodum natura humana trahitur per generationem absque imputatione naturae Adami, sic trahi per generationem defectus naturae humanae absque imputatione peccati actualis Adami. Trahitur nempe vitium naturae per actum naturae, non per actum Dei imputantis nobis peccatum Adami, & hos defectus infligentis.
latin.409: Adjunxisti alia eiusdem Thomae verba in quibus occurrit verbum imputandi, quod tu majusculis literis pinxisti. Subit mirari qui in caeteris controversiis Thomae Aquinatis, aliorumque scholasticorum Pontificiorum authoritatem nullo loco habent, in hac quaestione ea apud eos niti qui eam ipsi quoque contemnunt: nempe dogma istud de imputatione peccati actualis Adami omnibus hominibus nec antiquum est, & non aliunde primum fluxit quam ex lacunis quorundam scholasticorum, quos ne nominare quidem Lombardus Thomae magister, adeo obscuri erant, voluit. Thomas autem quamvis & imputandi verbo usus sit & tuae causae in speciem favere videatur, tamen revera abest a tua sententia haud parum, & mirum est te id non vidisse in his ipsis verbis quae citas, Adam, inquit, peccans vitavit naturam humanam, sed postmodum in aliis Natura vitiata (non igitur imputatio peccati actualis Adae) inficit personam, dum scilicet genito imputatur ad culpam NATURAE VITIUM propter voluntatem primi parentis, ut dictum est. Nonne vides verbi imputatur nominativum esse naturae vitium? dabis autem proculdubio mihi vitium naturae non esse peccatum actuale Adami, quod Thomas constanter docet fuisse peccatum personae. Nempe omnis in eo erat Thomas ut ostenderet quomodo ista nobis inhaerens naturae infectio seu vitium culpae rationem habere possit, cum sit involuntaria. Affirmat igitur ut actus per membrum exercitus habet rationem culpae & imputatur membro propter voluntatem non ipsius membri sed totius personae, sic vitium tractum ab Adamo & genito inhaerens culpae rationem habere & imputari genito ad culpam, non propter voluntatem geniti cuius respectu involuntarium est, sed propter voluntatem primi parentis. Itaque addidit ut dictum est, nempe verbis praecedentibus quae nos a te citata expendimus. Ausim affirmare imputationem peccati actualis Adami toti eius posteritati & inflictionem privationis justitiae originalis omnibus hominibus in poenam illius peccati imputati ignotas fuisse Thomae Aquinati, & possem id si opus esset necessariis argumentis demonstrare.
latin.410: Tertiam similitudinem petis a corpore civili. Ea bimembris est. Primum enim nobis ob oculos constituis Regem inferentem bellum vicinae genti, qui non solum ipse qui inferre voluit, & in consilio decrevit, & armis persecutus est, habetur pro hoste, sed etiam omnes subditi, quorum plerique nec voluerunt, nec consenserunt huic bello, & quanquam non agunt, & domi manent, si tamen in manus hostium veniant, excipiuntur incauti, concutiuntur, & jure belli interficiuntur. Attende, quaeso, quam non quadret haec similitudo. Principio si admittatur, fatendum erit, quemadmodum ab hoste capiuntur, & necantur qui nec bellum probant, nec in id consentiunt, nec ullo modo consilii Regis sunt participes, sic etiamsi nihil in nobis esset vitii, atque a peccato voluntas nostra abhorreret, tamen nobis imputari peccatum actuale Adami: quod qui tecum sentiunt multi non audent fateri. Deinde, consequens esset non solum primum peccatum Adami, sed reliqua etiam eius peccata actualia nobis esse imputanda: quippe cum generis humani caput fuerit quamdiu vixit. Tertio, si peccatum Capitis imputatur corpori, cur non etiam peccatum corporis imputetur capiti? nam si Adam & reliqui homines unum simul corpus sive totum constituunt, quam toti corpori membra singula conveniunt, tam etiam singulorum membrorum attributa conveniunt toti.
latin.411: Corpus enim non est unum membrum, sed multa: nec si pes caput non est, consequens est pedem non esse ex corpore. Imputatur autem toti corpori non modo quod caput facit, sed etiam quod pes. Itaque cum populum suum Deus consideraret ut unum corpus in deserto, toti populo ob unius Achan, qui populi illius caput non erat, iratus est. Si ergo omnes homines coalescunt cum Adamo in unum corpus, non unius Adami unum peccatum, sed omnia Adami, omnia aliorum hominum peccata toti corpori imputanda sunt. Quod tamen nec Apostolus, nec tu secundum Apostolum probas. Quarto, quid obstat quominus haec similitudo accommodetur etiam aliis stirpibus & parentibus respectu posterorum? Exempli causa, cur Noachus etiam non sit secundi mundi caput, Abrahamus Israelitarum, & ita de reliquis; unde magna exurget moles peccatorum imputandorum? Caput enim dicitur Adamus, & regi comparatur, non quia primus homo fuit, sed quia ab eo ducimus originem. Negatione relationis ad priorem ad nos minime refertur, sed relatione, quam generando sibi acquisivit, ad posteros. Quinto, si quis in manus hostium incidat quem certo noverint a bello fuisse & voluntate, & opere alienum, nec in id consensisse, hunc si interficiunt innocentem, mihi immanes & crudeles esse videntur. Alioqui qua Regis est mens bellum inferentis, eadem praesumitur esse mens omnium subditorum. Transfugis autem, iisque qui se dedunt, parci solet.
latin.412: Sexto, Rex bellum infert vicinae genti non per se solum, sed per subditos. Ipse imperat, subditi exequuntur. Ipse est causa principalis, subditi instrumentalis: ac illi ipsi, qui bello se non immiscent, subditi tenentur parere Regi, eumque pro viribus tueri & juvare. Adamus vero peccavit solus, ipse sibi, non nobis peccatum illud suum imperavit; ipse solus quod sibi imperavit, mandavit executioni, & opere perfecit. Posterorum nemo actioni illi interfuit, aut mentem manumve admovit suam. Non igitur ipse causa principalis fuit illius peccati, posteri causae instrumentales. Non ad committendum illud peccatum nos ei ut membra, ut organa, ut subditi, vel famuli accommodavimus, sed ipse solus, ut tunc extabat in rerum natura, ita peccatum illud per se ipsum commisit, nec posterorum quisquam illi adfuit. Bellum est commune Regis & subditorum opus, fitque a corpore regni: peccatum actuale Adami, ut tu ipse loqueris, unius personae fuit.
latin.413: Septimo, peccati imputatio, & poenae inflictio, actiones sunt judiciariae. Fieri debent a judice secundum leges. Lex autem est, Anima quae peccaverit ipsa morietur. Non feret iniquitatem filii pater, nec patris filius. Contra in bello leges silent, &, ut in statu perturbato, omnia vi fiunt: nec finis est ut fiat justitia, sed victoria, cuius causa gens cui bellum infertur in id unum intenta est, ut inferenti incommodet. Quoniam autem Regis potentia in subditorum multitudine & opibus sita est, eam ut atterant, & imminuant, & evertant, subditos Regi pro viribus, & bonis, & vita spoliare conantur: in quo scopus est & regi aegre facere, illique incommodare, & se tueri, ac opibus augere. Deus vero cum peccatum hominibus imputat & vindictam exercet, Judicis partibus fungitur.

pass_a.408: Placeus: the rest the learned man adds needs little refutation if you recall p. 163. When he opposed the assertion that Adam's will was the will of all, he did not take its sense to be that the volition Adam exercised about the forbidden tree is imputed to everyone. Thomas's following words must not be skipped: as actual sin (a person's) is drawn to the several members by some personal act, so original sin is drawn to individual men by nature's act—generation. He distinguishes both in Adam—person and nature—so original means corruption arisen from actual sin. Therefore he did not want the person's actual sin imputed to us, nor even nature's vice as it stuck in Adam: otherwise Seth's generation would also be imputed, being an act of nature. Placeus's sentence: as human nature is drawn by generation without imputing Adam's nature, so nature's defect is drawn by generation without imputing Adam's actual sin—by nature's act, not by God imputing Adam's sin and inflicting these defects.
pass_a.409: The opponent capitalized Thomas's verb "to impute." Placeus marvels that those who elsewhere give Thomas Aquinas and other Pontifical scholastics no place lean on them in this question though they themselves also contemn them: for the dogma of imputing Adam's actual sin to all men is not ancient, and first flowed from nowhere but the puddles of certain obscure scholastics whom even Lombard, Thomas's master, would not name. Though Thomas used "impute" and seems in appearance to favor the cause, in truth he is not a little distant: in the very words cited, Adam sinning vitiated human nature, but afterward a vitiated Nature infects the person when to the begotten is imputed unto fault NATURE'S VICE on account of the first parent's will—so the nominative of what is imputed is nature's vice, not Adam's actual person-sin. Thomas's whole aim was only to show how that inhering involuntary infection can have fault's nature—as an act through a member is imputed from the whole person's will, so the drawn vice from the first parent's will. Immediate imputation of Adam's actual sin to all posterity and infliction of privation of original justice as penalty of that imputed sin were unknown to Thomas Aquinas.
pass_a.410: Third likeness from the civil body: a King making war is held an enemy not only himself but all subjects—most unwilling, at home—yet if caught they are killed by right of war. Placeus: it does not fit. (1) Admit it and even with no vice in us and a will abhorring sin Adam's actual sin would still be imputed—which many who feel with the opponent dare not confess. (2) Then not only the first but all Adam's later actual sins would be imputed while he lived as head of the race. (3) If the Head's sin is imputed to the body, why not the body's to the head, since if Adam and the rest make one whole, members' attributes suit the whole as members suit the body.
pass_a.411: The body is not one member but many; the foot is of the body though not the head, and what the foot does is imputed to the whole body too. So when God considered his people as one body in the desert and was angry with the whole for one Achan—who was not that people's head—then if all men coalesce with Adam into one body, not one sin of one Adam but all Adam's and all other men's sins would have to be imputed to the whole, which neither the Apostle nor the opponent according to the Apostle allows. Fourth: why not fit this likeness also to other stocks—Noah as head of the second world, Abraham of the Israelites, and so of the rest—whence a great mass of sins to be imputed would arise? Adam is called head and compared to a king by the origin-relation he acquired to posterity by generating, not merely because he was first. Fifth: if enemies kill someone they know was alien to the war in will and deed, that seems monstrous; otherwise the King's war-mind is presumed the subjects' mind, yet deserters and those who surrender are usually spared.
pass_a.412: Sixth: a King makes war on a neighboring people not by himself alone but through subjects. He commands, they execute; he is principal cause, they instrumental; and even those who do not mix in the war are bound as subjects to obey the King and guard and help him with their strength. But Adam sinned alone: he commanded that sin of his to himself, not to us; he alone what he commanded himself put into execution and finished in deed. None of posterity shared in that action or put mind or hand to it. Therefore he was not the principal cause of that sin with posterity as instrumental causes. We did not fit ourselves to him as members, organs, subjects, or servants to commit that sin, but he alone, as he then stood in the nature of things, committed it by himself, and none of posterity was with him. War is the common work of King and subjects done by the kingdom's body; Adam's actual sin, as the opponent himself speaks, was of one person.
pass_a.413: Seventh: imputation of sin and infliction of penalty are judicial actions. They ought to be done by a judge according to laws. And the law is: The soul that has sinned, it shall die. The father shall not bear the son's iniquity, nor the son the father's. On the contrary in war the laws are silent, and, as in a disturbed state, all things are done by force: nor is the end that justice be done, but victory, for whose sake the people on whom war is made are intent on this one thing—to harm the one making it. And since the King's power lies in the multitude and wealth of subjects, they strive to wear down, diminish, and overthrow it by spoiling the King's subjects of strength and goods and life. But God, when he imputes sin to men and exercises vengeance, plays a Judge's part. Tip before the eighth objection (Adam not actually father or in relation when he sinned) deepen.

408: The rest the learned man adds here does not seem to need refutation, especially if you remember, candid reader, what we said above at p. 163. When I opposed the assertion that Adam's will was the will of all, I did not think its sense was that the volition Adam exercised about the forbidden tree is imputed to all. Thomas's following words which you wrote out, though they contain truth, must not be passed by. And just as actual sin, which is a person's sin, is drawn to the several members by some personal act, so original sin is drawn to individual men by the act of nature which is generation. Again he distinguishes actual from original, and wants both to have been in Adam: that of the person, this of nature. So by original he must mean the corruption arisen from actual sin. Therefore he did not want the person's actual sin imputed to us—nor even nature's vice as it stuck in Adam, as we shall soon see: otherwise the generation by which Adam begot Seth our second parent would also be imputed to us, since that, by Thomas's witness, was an act of nature. He adds: And so just as human nature is drawn by generation, so also by generation is traduced the defect of human nature which followed from the first parent's sin. Nothing truer. That is my sentence. Whence I conclude: as human nature is drawn by generation without imputation of Adam's nature, so the defect of human nature is drawn by generation without imputation of Adam's actual sin. Namely nature's vice is drawn by nature's act, not by an act of God imputing Adam's sin to us and inflicting these defects.
409: You added other words of the same Thomas in which the verb "to impute" occurs, which you painted in capital letters. One wonders that those who in other controversies give Thomas Aquinas and other Pontifical scholastics no place lean on them in this question though they themselves also contemn them: for that dogma of imputing Adam's actual sin to all men is not ancient, and first flowed from nowhere but the puddles of certain scholastics whom even Lombard, Thomas's master, would not name, so obscure were they. But though Thomas used the word "impute" and seems in appearance to favor your cause, in truth he is not a little distant from your sentence, and it is strange you did not see it in these very words you cite: Adam, he says, sinning vitiated human nature, but afterward in others a vitiated Nature (not therefore imputation of Adam's actual sin) infects the person, namely when to the one begotten is imputed unto fault NATURE'S VICE on account of the first parent's will, as was said. Do you not see that the nominative of "is imputed" is nature's vice? And you will doubtless grant me that nature's vice is not Adam's actual sin, which Thomas constantly teaches was a person's sin. For Thomas's whole aim was to show how that infection or vice of nature inhering in us can have the nature of fault though involuntary. So he affirms that as an act exercised through a member has the nature of fault and is imputed to the member because of the will not of the member itself but of the whole person, so the vice drawn from Adam and inhering in the begotten has the nature of fault and is imputed to the begotten unto fault, not because of the begotten's will in respect of which it is involuntary, but because of the first parent's will. So he added "as was said"—namely in the preceding words we weighed from your citation. I would dare affirm that imputing Adam's actual sin to all his posterity and inflicting privation of original justice on all men as penalty of that imputed sin were unknown to Thomas Aquinas, and I could prove it by necessary arguments if need were.
410: You seek a third likeness from the civil body. It is two-membered. First you set before our eyes a King making war on a neighboring people, who is held an enemy not only himself—he who willed to make it, decreed it in counsel, and pursued it with arms—but also all subjects, most of whom neither willed nor consented to this war, and though they do not act and stay at home, if they come into the enemies' hands they are caught unawares, shaken, and by right of war killed. Mark, I pray, how this likeness does not fit. First, if it is admitted, it must be confessed that as those who neither approve the war nor consent to it nor share the King's counsel are taken and slain by the enemy, so even if there were no vice in us and our will abhorred sin, Adam's actual sin would still be imputed to us—which many who feel with you dare not confess. Next, it would follow that not only Adam's first sin but also his other actual sins must be imputed to us, since he was head of the human race as long as he lived. Third, if the Head's sin is imputed to the body, why not also the body's sin to the head? For if Adam and the rest of men constitute one body or whole together, as the several members suit the whole body, so also the attributes of the several members suit the whole.
411: For the body is not one member but many: and if the foot is not the head, it does not follow that the foot is not of the body. And what the head does is imputed to the whole body, and also what the foot does. So when God considered his people as one body in the desert, he was angry with the whole people for one Achan, who was not that people's head. If therefore all men coalesce with Adam into one body, not one sin of one Adam but all Adam's and all other men's sins must be imputed to the whole body. Yet neither the Apostle nor you according to the Apostle approve that. Fourth, what stands in the way of fitting this likeness also to other stocks and parents respecting their posterity? For example, why should Noah not also be head of the second world, Abraham of the Israelites, and so of the rest—whence a great mass of sins to be imputed would arise? For Adam is called head and compared to a king not because he was the first man, but because we draw origin from him. He is not referred to us by negation of relation to a prior, but by the relation he acquired to posterity by generating. Fifth, if someone falls into enemies' hands whom they know for certain was alien to the war in will and deed and did not consent to it, if they kill that innocent man they seem to me monstrous and cruel. Otherwise the mind of the King making war is presumed to be the mind of all subjects. But deserters and those who surrender are usually spared.
412: Sixth. A King does not wage war on his neighbors by his own hand alone: he orders, and subjects carry out; he is the principal cause, they the instrumental—and even those who never take the field remain bound, as subjects, to obey him and to shield and aid him with their strength. Adam is not like that King. He sinned by himself. He laid that command of sin on himself, not on us; he alone executed what he had commanded himself and finished it in deed. No one among his posterity joined that action, nor lent mind or hand. So the scheme of principal and instrumental causes fails here: we did not lend ourselves to him as members, organs, subjects, or servants for committing that crime. He alone, as he then stood among the things that were, committed it through himself, and none of posterity stood with him at it. War is the shared work of King and subjects and is done by the kingdom's body; Adam's actual sin—as you yourself speak—was of one person only.
413: Seventh. To impute sin and to inflict a penalty are acts of a court. A judge must do them according to laws. And the law runs: The soul that has sinned shall itself die. A father shall not bear a son's iniquity, nor a son a father's. War is another regime: laws fall silent, and, as in a broken order, all things are done by force; nor is the end that justice be done, but victory—for whose sake the people under attack work only to harm the one who makes war. Because a King's strength sits in his subjects' numbers and wealth, they try to grind that strength down, diminish it, and overthrow it by stripping subjects of force and goods and life: both to vex the King and hurt him, and to save themselves and grow richer. God, when he charges men with sin and takes vengeance, does not play that war-game: he takes a Judge's part.
